topic: Peptides your body makes: why chilli burns. Capsaicin activates TRPV1 on pain-sensing nerves (Caterina et al., Nature 1997); TRPV1 is also activated by painful heat, so the brain reads 'hot' (Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2021, David Julius); activated nerve endings release substance P (and CGRP), an 11-amino-acid neuropeptide discovered in 1931 by von Euler and Gaddum in horse brain and gut and first called 'preparation P' (Suvas, J Immunol 2017); on skin these neuropeptides widen blood vessels causing redness, warmth and swelling (neurogenic inflammation; Gouin et al., Protein & Cell 2017)

$ why does chilli burn?

Your nerves mistake chilli for fire.

pain_nerve.log
STEP 01

Capsaicin

The hot molecule in chilli.

It switches on TRPV1, a sensor on pain nerves.

pain_nerve.log
STEP 02

Heat alarm.

TRPV1 also fires at painful heat.

Same switch. Your brain reads: HOT.

Nobel Prize 2021

pain_nerve.log
STEP 03

Substance P

The nerve releases this peptide. 11 amino acids.

Named in 1931 from “preparation P”.

OUTPUT

On skin, it widens blood vessels:
